The patient is a 73-year-old male with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer and COPD who is on hospital day 2 of an elective admission for cycle 4 of pembrolizumab and restaging imaging. He received pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks as planned yesterday and tolerated the infusion without any reaction. This morning he reports mild fatigue but feels otherwise well. He denies new cough, shortness of breath, fever, diarrhea, and rash. His appetite is good and he walked the ward hallway twice yesterday.

Vitals this morning are BP 128/76, HR 78, RR 16, temperature 98.4 F, and SpO2 96% on room air. He is comfortable and in no respiratory distress. Lung exam shows scattered end-expiratory wheeze at baseline without crackles. Heart rhythm is regular. The abdomen is soft and nontender, and there is no rash on the skin. CT chest obtained yesterday shows the right upper lobe mass is smaller than on the prior scan, with no new nodules and no sign of pneumonitis. TSH is 2.1 and creatinine is 0.9.

My impression is that his lung cancer is responding to pembrolizumab and that he is tolerating immunotherapy without immune-related adverse effects. COPD is stable. We will continue pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks, with the next dose due in 3 weeks, and repeat TSH and a metabolic panel before each cycle. He will be discharged home today and will follow up in the oncology clinic in 3 weeks. He was told to call right away for new cough, breathlessness, diarrhea, or rash.

Vitals were stable, CT chest showed a smaller right upper lobe mass with no pneumonitis, and TSH and creatinine were normal. The cancer is responding and there are no immune-related adverse effects. Pembrolizumab will continue every 3 weeks, with discharge today and oncology follow-up in 3 weeks.

HPI: The patient is an 80-year-old female with a history of hypertension who presents with 18 hours of right lower quadrant abdominal pain. The pain began around the umbilicus and moved to the right lower quadrant. She reports nausea and decreased appetite. She denies fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and dysuria. She is allergic to ibuprofen, which causes hives, so she has not taken any pain medication at home.

ROS: Positive for abdominal pain and nausea. Negative for fever, chest pain, and urinary symptoms.

Physical Exam: BP 142/78, HR 92, temperature 99.8 F, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air. She is uncomfortable but nontoxic. Abdomen is soft with focal tenderness and guarding at the right lower quadrant; no rebound or rigidity.

ED Course / Results: WBC 14.2, creatinine 1.0. Urinalysis is unremarkable. CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast shows acute appendicitis with a dilated appendix and periappendiceal fat stranding, no perforation or abscess. She received morphine 2 mg IV for pain and piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g IV. NSAIDs were avoided because of her ibuprofen allergy.

Medical Decision Making: Acute appendicitis confirmed on CT in an elderly patient with leukocytosis and no evidence of perforation. General surgery was consulted and agrees with operative management.

Disposition: Admitted to general surgery for appendectomy. She and her family understand the plan.

note:
Chief Complaint: Cut on left forearm

HPI: The patient is a 51-year-old female with type 2 diabetes who presents about 2 hours after cutting her left forearm with a kitchen knife while slicing a squash. She states the knife slipped and the cut bled a lot at first but stopped with pressure from a kitchen towel. She denies numbness, tingling, weakness of the hand, or trouble moving her fingers. She says she cannot remember her last tetanus shot. She takes metformin 500 mg twice daily and has no known drug allergies.

Health literacy: The patient reports she left school after eighth grade and has trouble reading medical forms. She asked that instructions be explained out loud. I used plain language, short sentences, and teach-back throughout the visit.

ROS: Negative for fever, numbness, tingling, and hand weakness. No other complaints.

Physical Exam: BP 136/82, HR 80, RR 16, temperature 98.3 F, SpO2 98% on room air. Alert and comfortable. On the volar left forearm there is a clean-edged 4 cm linear laceration through the dermis with visible subcutaneous fat, no exposed tendon or muscle, and no retained foreign body seen on exploration. Radial pulse is intact with capillary refill under 2 seconds. Sensation is intact in the median, ulnar, and radial distributions, and she has full finger flexion and extension against resistance.

ED Course / Results: Point-of-care glucose 168. The wound was anesthetized with lidocaine 1% 5 mL, irrigated with 500 mL of saline, and closed with 5 simple interrupted 4-0 nylon sutures. Tdap 0.5 mL IM was given. She tolerated the repair well.

Medical Decision Making: Simple laceration of the left forearm without tendon, nerve, or vascular injury, repaired in the ED. Tetanus status is unknown, so Tdap was given. Diabetes raises infection risk, so wound care instructions were reviewed carefully. Acetaminophen was started for pain.

Disposition: Discharged home. Start acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain, and continue metformin 500 mg twice daily. Keep the wound clean and dry for 24 hours, then wash gently with soap and water daily. Sutures out in 10 days at her clinic. She repeated back the return precautions in her own words: she will return for redness, swelling, pus, fever, or numbness. A picture handout was given.

She was discharged on acetaminophen as needed with metformin continued, suture removal in 10 days, and return precautions that she repeated back.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I have you down here as a 74-year-old female coming back after that spell with your arm and your speech, is that right?
Patient: Yes, that's right. I've been better, I think. I haven't had any more of those spells, no. I still get tired though.
Doctor: Okay. Let's go over what happened one more time so I know I have it right. About three weeks ago you had weakness in your left arm and your words came out slurred, and it lasted about ten minutes?
Patient: Yes. My arm just went heavy, like it was asleep, and my words came out thick. Then it went away. My daughter took me to the emergency room.
Doctor: Good. That kind of spell is called a TIA, a transient ischemic attack. Some people call it a mini stroke. It means blood flow to a part of the brain was blocked for a short time. Any headache, trouble seeing, or numbness since then?
Patient: No headache. No trouble seeing. No numbness.
Doctor: Any chest pain or heart racing?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Let's talk about your pills. What are you taking right now?
Patient: I take the baby aspirin every morning, and the pink pill for my blood pressure. That's lisinopril, I think. And the cholesterol pill at night, atorvastatin.
Doctor: Do you remember how strong the atorvastatin is?
Patient: Forty, I think. The bottle says forty.
Doctor: Good. I see in your chart you take aspirin 81 mg and lisinopril 10 mg each day. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, one each day. I never miss them.
Doctor: Good. I reviewed your tests. The MRI of your brain showed no stroke, which is good news. The ultrasound of the neck arteries showed a small amount of narrowing on the right, about 30 percent, which is not enough to need surgery. The heart ultrasound looked normal. Your LDL cholesterol was 128, which is too high for someone who has had a TIA. Your blood pressure today is 146/84, a bit high.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It is higher than where I want it. Your goal is under 130 over 80. Let me examine you now. Squeeze my fingers. Both hands feel equally strong. Smile for me, show me your teeth. Face is symmetric. Follow my finger with your eyes. Good. Say the sky is blue in Florida. Speech is clear. Walking looks steady. Your neurological exam is normal today.
Patient: That's good.
Doctor: Here is my impression. You had a TIA from small blood vessel disease, and the goal now is to prevent a real stroke. I'm going to increase your atorvastatin from 40 to 80 mg at night, keep the baby aspirin 81 mg, and raise your lisinopril from 10 to 20 mg every day. You'll wear a small heart monitor for 30 days to check for an irregular heartbeat, because that can also cause these spells. Come back in three months and we'll check your cholesterol and blood pressure again.
Patient: Okay. So the pills are more now?
Doctor: Yes. Tell me back in your own words what you're changing.
Patient: The cholesterol pill goes up to eighty at night, the blood pressure pill goes to twenty, and the aspirin stays the same. And I wear the heart monitor.
Doctor: Exactly right. And if you have another spell, with weakness, slurred speech, or face drooping, call 911 right away, don't wait.
Patient: Okay, I will.
summary: A 74-year-old female returned for follow-up of a TIA about three weeks ago, with ten minutes of left arm weakness and slurred speech, and has had no further spells but still feels tired. She denied headache, trouble seeing, numbness, and chest pain. MRI of the brain showed no stroke, carotid ultrasound showed about 30 percent right narrowing, LDL was 128, and blood pressure was 146/84 with a normal neurological exam. The TIA was attributed to small blood vessel disease. Atorvastatin was raised to 80 mg and lisinopril to 20 mg, aspirin 81 mg continues, and a 30-day heart monitor was arranged with return in three months. She repeated back the medication changes.

soap.subjective: 74-year-old female returning after a spell about three weeks ago of left arm weakness and slurred speech lasting about ten minutes, for which her daughter took her to the emergency room. Takes baby aspirin 81 mg every day, lisinopril 10 mg every day, and atorvastatin 40 mg at night.

The patient is a 66-year-old male with ileocolonic Crohn's disease who returns to clinic 3 weeks after a 5-day hospitalization for a Crohn's flare treated with intravenous steroids. He was discharged on prednisone 40 mg daily with a taper and is currently taking 15 mg daily. Over the past 5 days his abdominal cramping and loose stools have returned, now 6 watery stools a day, and he feels fatigued. He denies blood in the stool, fever, vomiting, and weight loss since discharge. He continues adalimumab 40 mg every other week without missed doses.

On exam, blood pressure is 124/74, heart rate 88, and temperature 98.6 F. He appears tired but not toxic. The abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant, no distension, no guarding, and no rebound. Labs today show hemoglobin 11.8, albumin 3.3, and C-reactive protein 32 mg/L. Stool C difficile testing from the hospital stay was negative.

This is a recurrent Crohn's flare as the prednisone taper has been lowered, in a patient who is still on adalimumab. I increased prednisone back to 40 mg daily with a slower taper and will continue adalimumab 40 mg every other week. I ordered fecal calprotectin and an MR enterography, and I will check in by phone in 1 week. He should go to the emergency department for fever, bloody stools, severe abdominal pain, or vomiting. Follow up in clinic in 3 weeks.

The assessment is a recurrent Crohn's flare despite adalimumab. Prednisone was increased back to 40 mg daily with a slower taper, adalimumab continues, fecal calprotectin and MR enterography were ordered, and follow-up is in 3 weeks.

note:
Chief Complaint: Right flank pain with nausea

HPI: The patient is an 18-year-old female with type 1 diabetes, asthma, and depression who presents with 6 hours of severe, colicky right flank pain radiating to the groin, with nausea and two episodes of vomiting. The pain started suddenly this morning, comes in waves, and is 9 out of 10 at its worst. She also notes burning with urination and urinary urgency since last night. She denies fever, chills, abdominal trauma, and gross blood in her urine. She was discharged from the hospital 3 weeks ago after an admission for diabetic ketoacidosis that followed a weekend of heavy drinking. She has not had a kidney stone before.

Medications and history: Home medications are insulin glargine at bedtime, insulin lispro with meals per sliding scale, and albuterol as needed. The patient first reported taking glargine 20 units nightly. Correction: after we reviewed her discharge paperwork, she confirmed that her dose was increased to 24 units nightly at discharge and she has been taking 24 units, not 20 units. At discharge naproxen 500 mg twice daily, which she had been taking for cramps, was stopped because it was no longer needed, and she says she has not taken it since. She also told us she stopped taking her sertraline 50 mg daily on her own 2 weeks ago because she felt it was not helping her depression. She has no known drug allergies.

Social history: She drinks about 8 to 10 drinks on weekend nights and had 3 drinks two nights ago. She denies other drug use and does not smoke. She denies any alcohol today and has no tremor, sweating, or anxiety.

ROS: Positive for flank pain, nausea, vomiting, dysuria, and urinary urgency. Negative for fever, chills, diarrhea, cough, wheezing, and chest pain.

Physical Exam: BP 118/72, HR 98, RR 18, temperature 98.9 F, SpO2 99% on room air. She is uncomfortable and moving constantly in the bed but is in no respiratory distress. Mucous membranes are slightly dry. Abdomen is soft, nondistended, with mild right lower quadrant tenderness and no rebound or guarding. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Lungs are clear with no wheezing. No tremor is noted.

ED Course / Results: Fingerstick glucose 168. WBC 11.8, creatinine 0.8. Beta-hydroxybutyrate and bicarbonate are normal, so there is no evidence of recurrent ketoacidosis. Urinalysis shows large blood, trace leukocyte esterase, negative nitrite, and 5 to 10 white blood cells per high power field. Urine hCG is negative. Blood alcohol level is undetectable. Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis shows a 5 mm obstructing stone at the right ureterovesical junction with mild hydronephrosis. She received normal saline 1 L IV, ketorolac 15 mg IV once, and ondansetron 4 mg IV, and her pain improved to 3 out of 10.

Medical Decision Making: Right ureteral stone with mild hydronephrosis in a patient with type 1 diabetes. The stone is small and should pass with conservative management. She has no fever, only mild leukocytosis, and the urine is not consistent with infection, so antibiotics are not needed. Renal function is normal, so ketorolac was acceptable. Her diabetes is stable with no ketoacidosis. Heavy alcohol use and its role in her recent admission were discussed, and brief counseling was given.

Disposition: Discharged home with urology follow-up in 1 week. Start ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 hours as needed with food for 5 days and ondansetron 4 mg every 8 hours as needed for nausea. Continue insulin glargine 24 units at bedtime and insulin lispro with meals. Naproxen remains stopped and should not be combined with ibuprofen. She is advised to discuss restarting sertraline with her primary doctor. She should strain her urine, drink at least 2.5 liters of fluid daily, and return for fever, uncontrolled pain or vomiting, or inability to urinate. She was given substance-use counseling materials.
summary: An 18-year-old female with type 1 diabetes, asthma, and depression, discharged 3 weeks ago after diabetic ketoacidosis following heavy drinking, presented with 6 hours of colicky right flank pain, nausea, vomiting, burning with urination, and urinary urgency. She denied fever and chills. CT showed a 5 mm obstructing stone at the right ureterovesical junction with mild hydronephrosis, labs showed no recurrent ketoacidosis, and her pain improved after ketorolac, ondansetron, and fluids. She was discharged on ibuprofen and ondansetron with insulin glargine 24 units at bedtime continued, urology follow-up in 1 week, alcohol counseling, and strain-and-hydrate instructions.

This is a progress note on a 75-year-old male on hospital day three, admitted with Graves disease and thyrotoxicosis complicated by atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. He presented four days ago with weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance, and tremor and was found to have a suppressed TSH, less than 0.01, a free T4 of 4.1, a diffuse goiter, and a positive thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin. Overnight he had no chest pain, no shortness of breath, and no fever, and his heart rate has come down from 128 to 92 on metoprolol tartrate, started at 25 mg twice daily on admission. Methimazole was started at 20 mg daily, correction, that should be 30 mg daily, the order in the chart is 30 mg daily. Apixaban 5 mg twice daily was started on admission as well for a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2.

Vitals this morning blood pressure 142/78, heart rate 92 and irregularly irregular, respiratory rate 18, temperature 98.6, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. On exam he has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands, warm moist skin, a smooth diffuse goiter, mild lid lag, and no proptosis. Lungs are clear and there is no leg edema. Labs today white blood cell count 6.8, creatinine 1.0, potassium 4.1.

Now the social piece. He lives alone, his wife died two years ago, and his only family is a nephew in another state who calls weekly. He admits he sometimes skips pills and has no one to help with transportation to follow-up. He would not be safe going home on three new medications without help.

Continue methimazole 30 mg daily, metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily, and apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Recheck free T4, CBC, and liver function tests in one week because of methimazole. Social work, physical therapy, and a pharmacist pillbox teaching session today, and arrange home health nursing and transportation to the endocrine clinic in two weeks. Discharge when his heart rate stays below 100 and the support plan is in place, likely tomorrow. Discuss definitive therapy such as radioactive iodine at the clinic visit.

Telehealth video visit for diabetic retinopathy screening results and follow-up. The patient is a 70-year-old male with type 2 diabetes for 14 years and hypertension, connected from home through a secure video platform with good audio and video. Identity was confirmed verbally and he consented to the visit.

History per patient: He had retinal photographs taken at his primary care office last week as part of annual diabetic eye screening. The photographs were read by ophthalmology as moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes with no macular edema. He reports occasional mild blurring of distance vision that clears when he blinks. He denies floaters, flashes of light, sudden vision loss, eye pain, and double vision. His last hemoglobin A1c was 7.8%.

Medications and supplements per patient: metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and aspirin 81 mg daily. He also takes over-the-counter supplements: ginkgo biloba 120 mg daily for memory, fish oil 1000 mg daily, and a turmeric capsule daily. He has no known drug allergies.

Home measurements: Blood pressure 134/78 and heart rate 72 on his home cuff this morning. Fasting fingerstick glucose was 132 this morning. Using the acuity chart on his screening card, he reads the 20/30 line with each eye. A self-administered Amsler grid showed no distortion or missing areas.

Limited video exam: Both eyes appear symmetric with no redness, swelling, or discharge. Eyelids and pupils appear normal in room light, extraocular movements look full when he follows my finger on camera, and there is no ptosis. A dilated retinal exam cannot be done by video.

Impression and plan: Moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy without macular edema in a patient with type 2 diabetes and hypertension. I will refer him to ophthalmology for an in-person dilated exam with OCT within 4 weeks. I advised him to stop ginkgo biloba because of added bleeding risk with aspirin and the potential for bleeding in the eye; fish oil and turmeric may continue. Continue metformin, lisinopril, and aspirin at current doses. Goal blood pressure is below 130/80, and we will repeat hemoglobin A1c in 3 months. He should call right away or go to the emergency department for sudden vision loss, a curtain over his vision, new floaters, or eye pain.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. Please have a seat. I have you down as a 67-year-old female here to go over your blood sugar and cholesterol results. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, doctor. I'm so nervous. My sister got diabetes last year and I keep thinking I'm next. Am I going to get diabetes? Will I need insulin? Can I ask a few questions before we start?
Doctor: Of course, ask as many as you like. Your A1c came back at 6.1 percent, which is in the prediabetes range, so you do not have diabetes right now. Let's go through your history first. Any increased thirst, passing a lot of urine, or blurry vision?
Patient: No, none of that. No extra thirst, no blurry vision. I do feel tired sometimes. And my feet tingle a little at night. Is that from the sugar?
Doctor: Tingling can have several causes, and with an A1c of 6.1 it is less likely to be from sugar. We will check your B12 level. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or swelling in your legs?
Patient: No chest pain. No swelling. I get a bit out of breath on stairs, but I think that's just my weight. Should I worry about that?
Doctor: We will keep an eye on it. Tell me which medicines you take.
Patient: Let me think. Lisinopril 20 mg for the pressure, once in the morning. Atorvastatin, I take 10 mg at night.
Doctor: Is that right? Your chart says 20.
Patient: Oh, wait, let me look at the photo of the bottle on my phone. You're right, it says 20 mg. I misread it, sorry. And aspirin 81 mg every day, omeprazole 20 mg for heartburn, and vitamin D, 2000 units.
Doctor: Thanks for checking. So lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg at night, aspirin 81 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and vitamin D3 2000 units daily.
Patient: Yes. Oh, and I stopped the amlodipine last month because my ankles were puffy. My other doctor said that was okay.
Doctor: Good to know, and the swelling is gone now?
Patient: Yes, it's gone. Is it dangerous that I stopped it?
Doctor: No, your pressure is acceptable today. Now your numbers. Fasting glucose was 112, A1c 6.1 percent. LDL 138, HDL 38, triglycerides 210. Blood pressure today is 138/84, weight 196 pounds, BMI 33, and waist 99 centimeters. On exam your heart is regular, lungs are clear, there is no swelling in your legs, the sensation in both feet is normal on the monofilament test, and you have some darkening of the skin on the back of your neck called acanthosis nigricans.
Patient: Oh no. What does that mean? Is it my fault? Could I have prevented this?
Doctor: It is not your fault. Genes matter a lot. Putting it together, you have prediabetes and metabolic syndrome, which means a cluster of belly weight, high triglycerides, low HDL, and borderline blood sugar and pressure. It raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease, but it is very treatable, and you can lower that risk by up to half with lifestyle changes.
Patient: Half? Really? What do I have to do? Do I have to give up all sugar? Can I still eat fruit?
Doctor: Fruit is fine. Here is the plan. First, aim to lose about 14 pounds, which is 7 percent of your weight, with walking 150 minutes a week, and a Mediterranean style diet. I will refer you to the diabetes prevention program and a dietitian. Second, I am going to increase your atorvastatin from 20 to 40 mg at night because your LDL is 138. Third, I want you to stop the aspirin 81 mg. At your age, with no heart attack or stroke before, the bleeding risk is bigger than the benefit. Continue lisinopril 20 mg, omeprazole 20 mg, and vitamin D3.
Patient: Stop the aspirin? Are you sure? My neighbor takes it every day.
Doctor: I am sure. The guidelines changed, and your risk of stomach bleeding is higher than the benefit. We will also check a B12 level, a liver panel in 6 weeks after the statin change, and repeat your A1c and lipid panel in 3 months.
Patient: Okay. Let me say it back. Walk 150 minutes, lose 14 pounds, atorvastatin goes up to 40, no more aspirin, keep the pressure pill and the others, and blood tests in 6 weeks and 3 months.
Doctor: Perfect. Come back in 3 months, and call sooner if you notice excessive thirst or urination, chest pain, or leg swelling.
Patient: Thank you. I feel better knowing the plan.
summary: A 67-year-old female came to discuss an A1c of 6.1 percent and was anxious and asked many questions. She denied thirst and blurry vision, chest pain, and leg swelling, but reported tiredness and tingling feet. Fasting glucose was 112, LDL 138, HDL 38, triglycerides 210, BP 138/84, BMI 33, and exam showed acanthosis nigricans. She was diagnosed with prediabetes and metabolic syndrome. Atorvastatin was increased from 20 to 40 mg and aspirin was stopped, with lifestyle changes, a diabetes prevention program, a dietitian, B12 and liver testing, and repeat A1c and lipids in 3 months.

The patient is a 68-year-old male with hypertension who presents to the infectious disease clinic with a painful rash on the left side of his chest that began 3 days ago. He first noticed burning pain along his left ribs 2 days before any rash appeared, followed by clustered blisters over the same band of skin. The pain is 6 out of 10 and keeps him awake at night. He denies fever, headache, eye involvement, and facial rash, and he reports no weakness in his arms or legs. He has no known allergies and has never received the shingles vaccine. He has had no contact with anyone with chickenpox.

Temperature is 98.7 F, BP 134/80, HR 76. He looks comfortable. There is a band of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the left T6 dermatome from the mid back to the sternum, with a few crusted lesions and no new vesicles, no secondary bacterial infection, and no lesions crossing the midline. Neurologic exam is nonfocal and there is no rash on the face or around the eye.

Impression is herpes zoster, left T6 dermatome, within the antiviral treatment window. I started valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for 7 days and gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime for nerve pain. He was counseled to keep the lesions covered, avoid contact with infants, immunocompromised people, and anyone who has not had chickenpox until the lesions crust, and wash his hands often. He should call for fever, spreading redness, eye pain, or vision changes. We will recheck him in 2 weeks and give the recombinant zoster vaccine series after the rash resolves.

Doctor: Hi, good to see you again. I have you down as a 37-year-old male here for kidney stone follow-up, right?
Patient: Yes. Two weeks ago I had terrible pain in my left side and went to the ER. They said I had a 6 millimeter stone. I took the tamsulosin, 0.4 mg every day, and drank a ton of water, and it passed five days ago. I caught it in the strainer like you told me.
Doctor: Great. How have you felt since it passed?
Patient: Much better. I get a little dull ache in my left side sometimes, but that's all. No blood in my urine anymore. No fever, no burning when I pee, and no nausea.
Doctor: Good. The stone analysis came back, and it is a calcium oxalate stone. That is the most common kind. Let's go over what you take. Any medicines or supplements?
Patient: I took ibuprofen 600 mg for the pain, but only during the attack. For supplements I take vitamin C, 1000 mg every day, for my immune system, a calcium pill, 500 mg, a fish oil, and protein powder, two scoops a day after the gym.
Doctor: Okay, that helps a lot. Vitamin C in that dose can turn into oxalate in the body and make the urine more likely to form stones, so I want you to stop the vitamin C. The calcium is fine. It actually helps if you take it with meals, because it binds oxalate in the gut. The protein powder, I would cut down to one scoop a day, because too much animal protein raises stone risk.
Patient: Wow, I didn't know that. I thought all that stuff was healthy.
Doctor: It is easy to do. Let me check you. Blood pressure is 126/78, pulse 70. There is no tenderness over your kidneys. Your creatinine from today is 0.9, so your kidney function is normal, and your urinalysis is clean, with no blood. The renal ultrasound we did today shows no hydronephrosis and no leftover stones.
Patient: That's a relief.
Doctor: Yes. So my impression is a calcium oxalate kidney stone that has passed with no complications. To lower the chance of another one, I want you to drink enough to make about 2.5 liters of urine a day, cut back on salt, and stop the vitamin C. I am also ordering a 24-hour urine collection to look at the chemistry, and we will see you in 3 months with another ultrasound. If you ever get severe pain, fever, or blood in your urine, come in or go to the ER.
Patient: Okay, got it. Stop the vitamin C, drink more water, less salt, one scoop of protein, the 24-hour urine, and see you in 3 months.
summary: A 37-year-old male returned for follow-up of a 6 millimeter left kidney stone that passed five days ago, with only an occasional dull ache and no blood in his urine, fever, burning with urination, or nausea. Stone analysis showed calcium oxalate. He takes over-the-counter supplements including vitamin C 1000 mg daily, calcium 500 mg, fish oil, and protein powder. Vitals were normal, creatinine was 0.9, urinalysis was clean, and renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis or residual stones. He was told to stop vitamin C, cut back on protein powder and salt, and drink more fluid, with a 24-hour urine collection and follow-up in 3 months.

The patient is a 54-year-old female seen in pulmonology clinic for follow-up 3 months after an unprovoked pulmonary embolism. She has been taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily since completing the initial higher-dose phase and reports no missed doses. On review of her supplements, she takes St. John's wort 300 mg daily for mood, which she started 2 weeks ago.

Vitals are BP 122/74, HR 72, RR 14, and SpO2 98% on room air at rest and 96% after walking the hallway. Lungs are clear. Heart sounds are regular with no murmur. Legs show no edema or calf tenderness. Hemoglobin today is 13.4 and creatinine is 0.8.

Impression is unprovoked pulmonary embolism, clinically improving on anticoagulation, with mild residual exertional dyspnea. St. John's wort lowers apixaban levels and raises the risk of clot recurrence, so I advised her to stop it and discuss mood treatment with her primary care doctor. She will continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily, and we discussed extended therapy given the unprovoked event. I ordered a transthoracic echocardiogram, and a ventilation-perfusion scan if the dyspnea persists. Return in 3 months.
